newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Defence minister defends military reform.
newsitem.headline: Defence minister defends military reform.

text.p: Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev on Friday shrugged off criticism of plans to radically reform Russia's armed forces by saying it was the only way to save the struggling military from final collapse.
"To save the armed forces for Russia, one has to reform them immediately and deeply," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Sergeyev as saying.

President Boris Yeltsin has ordered the defence ministry to cut troop numbers by 500,000 to 1.2 million by the end of next year in a series of steps meant to turn the demoralised military into a leaner and more effective fighting force.

Ousted security aide Alexander Lebed said he was not optimistic about the new reforms. Sacked defence minister Igor Rodionov and Lev Rokhlin, head of the lower house of parliament's defence committee, opened fire on policy overall.

"The president and prime minister's political approach to the problem (of military reform) destabilises the situation," Rodionov, sacked by Yeltsin in May for failing to carry out reforms, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper in an interview.
"I cannot understand why our leadership is so irresponsible about military reforms. We still have no doctrine, no concept, no programme and, that means, no everyday plans."

Rodionov said a "fifth column" could be trying to denigrate the armed forces. He did not say who he meant by this but said such saboteurs did not include military personnel and urged servicemen to be patient.
But Sergeyev insisted that the time for reforming Russia's military machine was ripe.
"It's the right time for military reform," he said. "The reform will be more difficult to carry out tomorrow and will become impossible later."

The armed forces, heavily funded in Soviet times, are now in disarray. They were defeated by separatist rebels in Chechnya, many soldiers have not been paid for months, corruption is rife and living conditions are getting worse.
Defence spending for 1997 was set at 88.3 trillion roubles ($15.3 billion) but later reduced under budget cuts. Officials say the military has so far received only 22 trillion roubles.
A mutiny is widely ruled out, although Rodionov said 95,000 officers had no homes and lived in railway carriages, garages, tents or their workplaces.
Yeltsin's decrees, issued on Wednesday, have not been published in full but the Kremlin gave some details on Friday.

Strategic missile troops, military space forces and military space air defence troops are to be regrouped into one separate force called the strategic missile troops. Air defence troops will be merged with the air force.
Funds raised from privatising some military organisations and from sales of property and equipment to be taken out of service are to be set aside to help the discharged servicemen.
"The whole point of reforms is adjusting the armed forces to the military and political reality and to the economic capability of the state," Sergeyev said.
Kremlin defence aide Yuri Baturin said the first 200,000 personnel would be discharged by the end of this year.
This would include 50,000 officers and cuts in personnel in military road construction groups, special engineering units and other building groups.
The Defence Ministry's central administration will be limited to 12,000 -- one percent of the armed forces.
